chapters.title: The Song of Songs
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 1

1The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.

2Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth!
For your love is better than wine;

3your oils are good for fragrance;
your name is oil poured out;
therefore the young women love you.

4Draw me after you; let us run.
The king has brought me into his chambers.
We will exult and rejoice in you;
we will praise your love more than wine.
Rightly do they love you.

5I am black and lovely,
daughters of Jerusalem,
like the tents of Kedar,
like the curtains of Solomon.

6Do not stare at me because I am dark,
because the sun has looked on me.
My mother's sons were angry with me;
they made me keeper of the vineyards;
my own vineyard I have not kept.

7Tell me, you whom my soul loves,
where you pasture your flock,
where you make it lie down at noon;
for why should I be like one who is veiled
beside the flocks of your companions?

8If you do not know,
most beautiful among women,
follow the tracks of the flock,
and pasture your young goats
beside the shepherds' tents.

9I compare you, my darling,
to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots.

10Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments,
your neck with strings of beads.

11We will make you ornaments of gold,
studded with silver.

12While the king was at his table,
my nard gave its fragrance.

13My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh
that lies all night between my breasts.

14My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms
in the vineyards of En-gedi.

15How beautiful you are, my darling,
how beautiful!
Your eyes are doves.

16How handsome you are, my beloved,
how pleasant!
Our couch is green;

17the beams of our house are cedar;
our rafters are cypress.

Notes

  • v1 "The Song of Songs" — the Hebrew way of saying the greatest of songs, as "the holy of holies" is the most holy place and "vanity of vanities" (Ecclesiastes 1:2) is utter vanity. "Which is Solomon's" — lishlomoh, "of Solomon": by him, for him, or about him; the Hebrew allows all three.

  • v2 "Let him kiss me… your love is better than wine" — she turns from "him" to "you" within one line, from speaking of him to speaking to him. "Your love" — dodekha, love given and shown, caresses (the same word in 4:10). The Greek reads the same letters as dadayikh, "your breasts."

  • v3 "your name is oil poured out" — shem and shemen, the same play of sound as Ecclesiastes 7:1.

  • v5 "I am black and lovely" — shechorah, "black," darkened by the sun (v6). The Hebrew and the Greek join the two words with "and," not "but." "The tents of Kedar" — the black goat-hair tents of Kedar, a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13).

  • v6 "my own vineyard I have not kept" — her brothers set her to work in their vineyards, and she has had no care for her own. The vineyard stands for herself again in 8:12.

  • v7 "you whom my soul loves" — her name for him; it returns four times in 3:1–4. "Like one who is veiled" — ote'yah, a woman wrapped in a veil, as the Greek has it. A veiled woman wandering among shepherds' camps could be taken for a woman of another sort (compare Tamar, Genesis 38:14–15).

  • v9 "my darling" — ra'yati, from re'a, "companion, friend"; his name for her, nine times in the Song.

  • v14 "En-gedi" — the spring in the desert above the Dead Sea where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1).

  • vv15–16 "How beautiful you are… How handsome you are" — he speaks and she answers in his own words (hinnakh yafah… hinnekha yafeh).

chapters.title: The Winter Is Past
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 2

1I am a flower of Sharon,
a lily of the valleys.

2Like a lily among thorns,
so is my darling among the young women.

3Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest,
so is my beloved among the young men.
In his shade I delighted to sit,
and his fruit was sweet to my taste.

4He brought me to the house of wine,
and his banner over me was love.

5Sustain me with raisin cakes;
refresh me with apples,
for I am sick with love.

6His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

7I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles or by the does of the field,
that you not stir up or awaken love
until it pleases.

8The voice of my beloved!
He is coming,
leaping over the mountains,
bounding over the hills.

9My beloved is like a gazelle
or a young stag.
He stands behind our wall,
gazing through the windows,
peering through the lattice.

10My beloved spoke and said to me:
"Arise, my darling, my beautiful one,
and come away,

11for the winter is past;
the rain is over and gone.

12The flowers appear on the earth;
the time of singing has come,
and the voice of the turtledove
is heard in our land.

13The fig tree ripens its green figs,
and the vines in blossom give their fragrance.
Arise, my darling, my beautiful one,
and come away.

14My dove, in the clefts of the rock,
in the hiding place of the cliff,
let me see your face,
let me hear your voice,
for your voice is sweet,
and your face is lovely."

15Catch the foxes for us,
the little foxes
that spoil the vineyards,
for our vineyards are in blossom.

16My beloved is mine, and I am his;
he pastures among the lilies.

17Until the day breathes
and the shadows flee,
turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle
or a young stag
on the cleft mountains.

Notes

  • v1 "a flower of Sharon" — chavatselet, a meadow flower whose kind is not known for certain (crocus, asphodel and narcissus have all been proposed); the Greek has "a flower of the plain," and Sharon is the coastal plain. "Rose" in older English Bibles has nothing in the word to support it. "Lily" — shoshannah, a lily or a lotus.

  • v4 "his banner over me was love" — diglo, "his banner," the standard each tribe camped under (Numbers 2:2): his sign is raised over her for all to see. The Greek has "set love in order over me."

  • v7 "by the gazelles or by the does of the field" — bitsva'ot, "by the gazelles," is spelled exactly as tseva'ot, "hosts," and ayelot hassadeh, "does of the field," sounds like El Shaddai: the oath is sworn by wild creatures in words that echo the names of God. The Greek read them "by the powers and by the strengths of the field." The same charge comes again, word for word, in 3:5.

  • v7 "until it pleases" — love is not to be roused before its own time.

  • v12 "the time of singing" — zamir, "singing" or "pruning," both of them spring; the Greek has "pruning."

  • v16 "My beloved is mine, and I am his" — in 6:3 the order turns around, and in 7:10 it becomes "I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me."

  • v17 "the cleft mountains" — harei vater: "the mountains of Bether," a place not otherwise known, or "mountains of cutting." Bater is the word for the halves of the animals cut in two at the covenant with Abram (Genesis 15:10). The Greek has "mountains of hollows."

chapters.title: Him Whom My Soul Loves
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 3

1On my bed by night
I sought him whom my soul loves;
I sought him, but did not find him.

2I will rise now and go about the city,
in the streets and in the squares;
I will seek him whom my soul loves.
I sought him, but did not find him.

3The watchmen found me
as they went about the city.
"Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"

4Scarcely had I passed them
when I found him whom my soul loves.
I held him, and would not let him go
until I had brought him into my mother's house,
into the room of her who conceived me.

5I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles or by the does of the field,
that you not stir up or awaken love
until it pleases.

6Who is this coming up from the wilderness
like columns of smoke,
perfumed with myrrh and frankincense,
with all the powders of the merchant?

7It is Solomon's own litter,
with sixty mighty men around it,
of the mighty men of Israel,

8all of them holding swords,
trained in war,
each with his sword at his thigh
against the terror of the night.

9King Solomon made himself a carriage
from the wood of Lebanon.

10He made its posts of silver,
its back of gold,
its seat of purple;
its inside was inlaid with love
by the daughters of Jerusalem.

11Go out, daughters of Zion,
and look on King Solomon,
with the crown with which his mother crowned him
on the day of his wedding,
on the day of the gladness of his heart.

Notes

  • vv1–4 "him whom my soul loves" — four times in four verses, her name for him from 1:7. She seeks him in the night and the city, and the search ends only when she finds him.

  • v4 "into my mother's house" — as Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent of his mother Sarah (Genesis 24:67); again in 8:2.

  • v5 — the charge of 2:7, word for word.

  • v6 "Who is this" — zot is feminine: "who is she?", or "what is this?", the litter (feminine mittah) of v7. The same question opens 8:5.

  • v9 "a carriage" — appiryon, found only here; the Greek translator rendered it phoreion, "litter," a word it closely resembles.

  • v10 "inlaid with love" — ratsuf ahavah: its inside laid with love, the work or the gift of the daughters of Jerusalem; the Greek reads the same.

  • v11 "the crown with which his mother crowned him" — a wedding crown, not the crown of rule. This is the only wedding the Song names.

chapters.title: A Garden Locked
chapters.html:
Song of Songs 4

1How beautiful you are, my darling,
how beautiful!
Your eyes are doves
behind your veil.
Your hair is like a flock of goats
streaming down from Mount Gilead.

2Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes
that have come up from the washing,
all of them bearing twins,
and not one among them has lost its young.

3Your lips are like a scarlet thread,
and your mouth is lovely.
Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate
behind your veil.

4Your neck is like the tower of David,
built in rows of stone;
a thousand bucklers hang on it,
all of them shields of mighty men.

5Your two breasts are like two fawns,
twins of a gazelle,
that graze among the lilies.

6Until the day breathes
and the shadows flee,
I will go to the mountain of myrrh
and to the hill of frankincense.

7You are altogether beautiful, my darling;
there is no blemish in you.

8Come with me from Lebanon, my bride;
come with me from Lebanon.
Look down from the peak of Amana,
from the peak of Senir and Hermon,
from the dens of lions,
from the mountains of leopards.

9You have taken my heart, my sister, my bride;
you have taken my heart with one of your eyes,
with one jewel of your necklace.

10How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride!
How much better is your love than wine,
and the fragrance of your oils than any spice!

11Your lips drip honey from the comb, my bride;
honey and milk are under your tongue;
the fragrance of your garments
is like the fragrance of Lebanon.

12A garden locked is my sister, my bride,
a spring locked, a fountain sealed.

13Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates
with the choicest fruits,
henna with nard,

14nard and saffron,
calamus and cinnamon,
with every tree of frankincense,
myrrh and aloes,
with all the finest spices —

15a fountain of gardens,
a well of living water,
and streams flowing from Lebanon.

16Awake, north wind,
and come, south wind!
Blow on my garden;
let its spices flow.
Let my beloved come to his garden
and eat its choicest fruits.

Notes

  • v1 "How beautiful you are, my darling, how beautiful! Your eyes are doves" — the words of 1:15, now opening a description of her from her eyes downward; vv1–3 come back almost word for word in 6:5–7.

  • v2 "all of them bearing twins" — every tooth matched with its pair, and none missing.

  • v4 "built in rows of stone" — letalpiyyot, found only here, and its meaning is uncertain: built in courses of stone, or built "for weapons" or "for trophies." The Greek takes it as a place name, Thalpioth.

  • v7 "no blemish in you" — mum, the blemish that bars a priest from serving and an animal from the altar (Leviticus 21:17–23; 22:20–21).

  • v8 "my bride" — kallah, six times in 4:8–5:1 and nowhere else in the Song. "My sister" (v9) is a word of closeness for a wife, not a word of kinship.

  • v9 "You have taken my heart" — libbavtini, a verb made from lev, "heart"; the Greek has the same, "you have hearted me." "With one of your eyes" — a single glance was enough.

  • vv10–11 "How much better is your love than wine" — he gives back her own words of 1:2–3: dodim, "love," better than wine, and the fragrance of oils. "Honey and milk" — the land "flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8), with the order turned around.

  • v12 "A garden locked… a spring locked" — the second word is gal, "spring" (or "heap"), one letter from gan, "garden"; the Greek has "garden" both times.

  • v13 "an orchard" — pardes, a Persian word for a walled park (Nehemiah 2:8; Ecclesiastes 2:5). The Greek renders it paradeisos, its word for Eden's garden in Genesis 2:8, from which English has "paradise."

  • vv15–16 "a well of living water… Let my beloved come to his garden" — the words of Genesis 26:19, flowing water. In v16 she answers, and in one line "my garden" becomes "his garden."
